senses.gloss:
vikalpa
(‘doubt,’ ‘choice’)
------------------------------------------
This word has several senses. When मनस् or the मिन्द् is defined as that part of the अन्तःकरण (inner organ) which is responsible for saṇkalpa and विकल्प, the word विकल्प stands for doubt.
In a more technical sense, it stands for an alternative or an option. If a Vedic passage declares that one can offer sacrifice with vrīhi (rice) or yava (barley), it is a विकल्प that gives a choice to the sacrificer.
The धर्मशास्त्रस् give many vikalpas or alternatives in the performance of certain rituals (vide Manusmṛti 3.267).
The Yogasūtras (1.9) uses the word विकल्प to indicate that wave of the मिन्द् which arises after hearing a word even though there is no corresponding real object outside. For instance, when we hear the word “Rāhu’s head,” the idea of a head that arises in the मिन्द् is a विकल्प because राहु (the planet) has only a head and no other part of the body.

vikṣepa
(‘throwing,’ ‘distracting’)
------------------------------------------
This is a technical word used in several senses.
In the न्याय philosophy, it is interpreted as ‘evasion’. When a person, who is involved in a disputation, finds himself on the losing side and tries to escape by saying that he has to go on some urgent business, it is called ‘vikṣepa’ (vide Nyāyasūtras 5.2.19).
In the Yogasūtras (1.30), the word is used to indicate those nine factors such as व्याधि (illness), प्रमाद (heedlessness) and अविरति (absence of renunciation), which act as अन्तरायस् or obstacles to the practice of योग.
In the Advaita Vedānta, it is one of the two śaktis (powers) of अविद्या (nescience). For instance, अविद्या covers the real nature of the rope as rope by its āvaraṇaśakti (covering power) and makes it appear as a snake by its vikṣepaśakti (power of projection).

Vikramāditya
(‘Sun of Valour’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu tradition and old legends describe a great and heroic king, विक्रमादित्य, who drove away foreigners (Śakas or Hūṇas), built an empire and ruled from उज्जयिनी as his capital.
There were nine great men of learning, generally called the Navaratnas (= nine gems), including कालिदास, धन्वन्तरि, वराहमिहिर and वररुचि, in his court under his patronage.
Later quite a few kings of the historical period assumed this name as a title.
The Vikramaśaka is reckoned from the year 57 B. C., probably the year of his चोरोनतिओन्. This śaka is commonly observed and used in North India.

Vikramaśīla
------------------------------------------
The विक्रमशील monastery is one of the three well-known centres of learning of ancient and medieval India, the other two being the तक्षशिला and the नालन्दा.
This Buddhist monastery which developed into a great centre of learning was established by the king Dharmapāla (reign A. D. 770-810) of the Pāla dynasty, ruling over Bihar and Bengal. The centre itself was named विक्रमशील monastery, the word ‘Vikramaśīla’ being a title of the king Dharmapāla.
It was located at the top of a hill, on the bank of the river गङ्गा in the Magadha country. This has been identified with the hill Pātharghāṭa near Bhāgalpur (in the Bihar State).
The spiritual head of the monastery was called Vajrācārya. The very first Vajrācārya was Buddhajñānapāda, a disciple of Haribhadra, the गुरु (spiritual preceptor) of Dharmapāla.
It grew into a mighty centre of learning, not only of बुद्धिस्म् but also of other branches of learning.
There were 108 cells set apart for Buddhist मोन्क्स्. Some were meant for the practice of tāntrik disciplines and others for living. These मोन्क्स् called paṇḍitas, were in charge of the various departments of the monastery.
Students would flock from all parts of the country and also from foreign countries, especially from Tibet.
Diplomas would be awarded to the proficient students, including the मोन्क्स्.
Many Sanskrit works were translated here into the Tibetan language.
The institution which was devoted to Mahāyāna बुद्धिस्म् had to face troubles created by Śrāvakas or bhikṣus from Siṁhaḷa who followed Hīnayāna.
The campus had six dvāras or Main gates, each under the charge of a dvārapaṇḍita, responsible for the admission of students as also to face the scholars of other schools and systems.
This wonderful institution was destroyed in A. D. 1205 by the Muslim invaders.
See also NĀLANDĀ and TAKṢAŚILĀ.
